s.d: to sow in addition to a previous sowing
s.g: to sow in addition; to sow on top of

s.d: to scatter seed over tilled ground{N:001}
s.c: In many languages there is a problem of translating σπείρω literally as ‘to scatter seed,’ since this is interpreted as an exceedingly wasteful manner of sowing, but unless one translates more or less literally and then provides some explanatory footnote, the parable loses much of its significance for many cultures.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the fleshy part on either side of the face
s.c: Though in many languages there is a specific term for ‘cheek,’ in some instances it may be necessary to use a phrase meaning ‘the side of the head’ or ‘the side of the face.’

s.d: to keep quiet, with the implication of preserving something which is secret
s.g: to keep quiet about; to say nothing about

s.d: the absence of noise
s.c: It is possible that σιγή in ⟦Revelation 8:1|Revelation 8:1⟧ does not refer to verbal silence.

s.d: iron
s.c: Since at the present time iron in some form is almost universal throughout the world, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for it. In some instances, in fact, it is such a dominant metal that it is known simply as ‘the metal.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:σίδηρος<SDBG:σίδηρος:000000>} ‘iron,’ {D:2.58}) pertaining to being made or consisting of iron

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city on the coast of Phoenicia

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Σιδών<SDBG:Σιδών:000000>} ‘Sidon,’ {D:93.577}) pertaining to Sidon

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Σιδών<SDBG:Σιδών:000000>} ‘Sidon,’ {D:93.577}) a person who lives in or is a native of Sidon
one who kills someone with intent and as a part of a plot
an intoxicating drink made from grain
s.c: Though σίκερα may have a generic meaning and thus refer to any type of intoxicating drink, in the NT it occurs only in ⟦Luke 1:15|Luke 1:15⟧, where it contrasts with wine and refers to intoxicating beverages made from grain. Distilled alcoholic beverages, such as whiskey, gin, and vodka, were not known in the ancient world.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian in the Jerusalem church and an associate of Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: generally regarded as the same person as {L:Σιλᾶς<SDBG:Σιλᾶς:000000>} ({D:93.339})

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the name for a system of water supply in Jerusalem; the pool of Siloam was probably the basin into which the water flowed

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a cloth or piece of leather wrapped by a workman around his waist or chest to protect his clothes
s.c: A σιμικίνθιον may be called in some languages ‘a workman’s cloth’ or ‘a workman’s cloth to protect clothing.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Simon Peter, one of the twelve apostles

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Simon the Zealot, one of the twelve apostles

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a brother of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of Judas Iscariot

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a tanner in Joppa

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a magician of Samaria

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a leper

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Pharisee

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a rocky mountain on the peninsula of Sinai

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: mustard plant, a large herb noted for its very small seeds and in some instances growing to a height of three meters (about ten feet)
s.c: Note that in ⟦Matthew 13:31|Matthew 13:31⟧ (and in the parallel passage ⟦Luke 13:19|Luke 13:19⟧) σίναπι is actually spoken of as a δένδρον tree, evidently a type of rhetorical hyperbole.|Though the mustard plant may not be known in certain areas of the world, the use of mustard as a condiment is widely known, and therefore it is often possible to speak of ‘a plant that produces mustard’ or ‘the plant used in making mustard.’ In order, however, to make the parable meaningful, it may be necessary to have some explanation of this plant in a footnote or glossary.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: linen cloth of good quality
s.c: In a number of languages there is no term for ‘linen,’ and though a word for ‘linen’ may be borrowed, what is important in the NT contexts in which σινδών occurs is primarily the quality of the cloth, not the material of which it was made. Accordingly, many translators have used an expression such as ‘fine cloth’ or ‘good cloth.’

s.d: to sift by shaking in a sieve
s.c: The expression ὑμᾶς τοῦ σινιάσαι ὡς τὸν σῖτον in ⟦Luke 22:31|Luke 22:31⟧ is clearly a type of figurative usage and in many languages must be translated as ‘to test you’ or ‘to test you so as to separate the good from the bad.’ In some languages, however, it may be more satisfactory to shift the figure from sifting to winnowing and hence translate ‘to winnow you like a farmer who separates the wheat from the chaff.’

s.d: pertaining to being well fed on grain and hence fattened
s.c: In ⟦Luke 15:27|Luke 15:27⟧ σιτευτός may, however, mean ‘valuable’ or ‘prize.’ This would simply be an extended meaning of σιτευτός in view of the resulting condition or value of a grain-fed animal. For this interpretation of σιτευτός in ⟦Luke 15:27|Luke 15:27⟧, see LN 65.8.

s.d: pertaining to being valuable or prized on the basis of its being well fed and fat (occurring in reference to a calf)
s.c: For another interpretation of σιτευτός in ⟦Luke 15:27|Luke 15:27⟧, see LN 44.2.

s.d: (a diminutive form of {L:σῖτος<SDBG:σῖτος:000000>} ‘grain,’ {D:3.41}, but not diminutive in meaning) any grain, but with the evident implication of its relevance as food
s.c: (See also LN 5.2.) On the basis of this one NT occurrence it is impossible to know whether the meaning of σιτία is ‘grain’ or ‘food,’ since in the phrase σιτία καὶ ποτά ‘food and drink’ (an expression occurring in a number of extrabiblical contexts), the term σιτίον contrasts solid with liquid nourishment.

s.d: (diminutive of {L:σῖτος<SDBG:σῖτος:000000>}[a] ‘wheat, grain,’ {D:3.41}, but without diminutive meaning and occurring primarily in the plural) food consisting principally of grain products
s.c: It is, of course, possible in ⟦Acts 7:12|Acts 7:12⟧ to understand the plural form as ‘grain’ (see LN 3.42), but the reference is probably to food made from grain, a common meaning of this term in Classical Greek.

s.d: any kind of edible grain, though generally referring to wheat

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: the plant of wheat
s.c: Elsewhere in the NT σῖτος, when used alone, refers to wheat as grain, but even in ⟦John 12:24|John 12:24⟧ τοῦ σίτου may be interpreted as a so-called ‘appositional genitive,’ that is, ‘seed which is wheat’ or ‘wheat seed.’|While in some parts of the world wheat as a grain or as a plant is not known, in almost all instances people are acquainted with wheat flour, and therefore it is often possible to translate ‘wheat’ as ‘flour plant’ or ‘plant the grain of which is used to make flour.’ In some languages, however, the only possible equivalent is ‘rice-like plant’ in which ‘rice-like’ means essentially ‘grass-like,’ while at the same time indicating edible grain.

s.d: pertaining to being well fed on grain and hence fattened
an appropriate portion or ration of food (a type of food allowance)
s.g: a due amount of food rations
s.c: It is possible to interpret σιτομέτριον in ⟦Luke 12:42|Luke 12:42⟧ as ‘the proper amount of food’ or ‘the food that was due them’ or ‘the food that should be given (to the servants).’ Since σιτομέτριον is a semantically complex term consisting of two quite distinct components, it is usually necessary to employ a phrase as a proper equivalent.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: Mount Zion, a hill within the city of Jerusalem

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the city of Jerusalem together with its people, particularly in poetic discourse; see also {D:11.66}
to refrain from speaking or talking
s.g: to keep quiet; to be silent

s.d: to lose or not have the ability to speak
s.g: to not be able to speak
s.c: It is possible that σιωπάω in ⟦Luke 1:20|Luke 1:20⟧ means only ‘to say nothing’ or ‘to remain silent’ (LN 33.117), in which case it would probably be better to reverse somewhat the order and translate ‘and you will not be able to speak but will remain silent until the day these things happen.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σιωπάω<SDBG:σιωπάω:000000>}[a] ‘to be silent,’ {D:33.117}) the process of becoming calm after a storm
s.g: to become calm; to become still
s.c: In a number of languages it is not possible to translate σιωπάω literally as ‘be still’ since this might imply continue to remain still. Since there is a change in state, it may be necessary to say become still or cease to be stormy.

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Change an Opinion Concerning Truth
s.d: to cause someone to no longer believe
s.g: to cause to give up believing; to make someone no longer believe
s.c: It is also possible to understand σκανδαλίζω in ⟦John 6:61|John 6:61⟧ as meaning ‘to cause offense’ (see LN 25.179).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκανδαλίζω ‘to cause to stumble,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause to sin, with the probable implication of providing some special circumstances which contribute to such behavior

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Offend, Be Offended
s.d: to cause someone to experience anger and/or shock because of what has been said or done
s.g: to cause someone to be offended; to offend
s.c: See discussion at LN 25.180.

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Change an Opinion Concerning Truth
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκανδαλίζομαι ‘to fall into a trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to give up believing what is right and let oneself believe what is false
s.g: to cease believing; to give up believing
s.c: It is also possible to understand σκανδαλίζομαι in ⟦Matthew 13:21|Matthew 13:21⟧ as meaning ‘to let oneself be led into sin’ or ‘to fall into sin as the result of unbelief.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: to fall into sin, with the implication of certain contributing circumstances
s.g: to sin; to fall into sin

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Offend, Be Offended
s.d: to be offended because of some action
s.g: to be offended; to take offense
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to be offended’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to be bitter against’ or ‘to be stung in the heart.’ In some languages, however, the closest equivalent for some contexts is simply ‘to be angered.’

s.d: a trap, probably of the type which has a stick which when touched by an animal causes the trap to shut
s.c: In ⟦Romans 11:9|Romans 11:9⟧ παγίς (LN 6.23), θήρα (LN 6.24), and σκάνδαλον would all seem to be completely parallel in structure and meaning. As a result, in a number of languages the three terms are reduced often to two, for example, ‘snare’ and ‘trap.’ If there are three different kinds of traps, then, of course, three terms can be used. In some cases, however, it may be preferable to use verbs to express the catching and trapping, and thus one may translate γενηθήτω ἡ τράπεζα αὐτῶν εἰς παγίδα καὶ εἰς θήραν καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον as in TEV, “may they be caught and trapped at their feasts; may they fall.”

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκάνδαλον[a] ‘trap,’ {D:6.25}) that which or one who causes someone to sin
s.g: that which causes someone to sin; one who causes someone to sin

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Offend, Be Offended
s.d: that which causes offense and thus arouses opposition
to make a hole in the ground and to remove earth with some sharp-edged intrument (for example, a pick or spade)
s.c: For another interpretation of σκάπτω in ⟦Luke 16:3|Luke 16:3⟧, see LN 43.3.

s.d: to dig into the ground, specifically in connection with turning over the earth for agricultural or gardening purposes
s.g: to till the ground; to dig
s.c: For another interpretation of σκάπτω in ⟦Luke 16:3|Luke 16:3⟧, see LN 19.55.

s.dp: Artifacts › Boats and Parts of Boats
s.d: a small boat which was normally kept aboard a larger ship and used by sailors in placing anchors, repairing the ship, or saving lives in the case of storms
s.c: In some languages σκάφη is equivalent to ‘rowboat’ or ‘lifeboat.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: limb of a human or animal that supports the body and is used for movement; the two human legs extend from the top of the thigh to the foot

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: clothing as a covering{N:001}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Jewish high priest
a collective for any kind of artifact which may be referred to by {L:σκεῦος<SDBG:σκεῦος:000000>}[a] ‘object, thing’ ({D:6.1})
s.c: Wherever possible, it is useful to employ a rather specific term if this is well known in a receptor language. For example, instead of ‘things of a ship’ one may use ‘ship’s gear’ or ‘ship’s rigging.’

s.d: any kind of instrument, tool, weapon, equipment, container, or property
s.c: The manner in which σκεῦος is translated depends in many instances upon the specific context. It may, of course, be rendered by a highly generic expression such as English ‘thing,’ but wherever the context refers to some particular type of object, it is preferable to employ a specific referent. In ⟦Acts 27:17|Acts 27:17⟧, for example, the reference of σκεῦος is generally understood to be the mainsail.

s.d: a highly generic term for any kind of jar, bowl, basket, or vase
s.c: In ⟦Acts 10:11|Acts 10:11⟧ and ⟦Acts 10:16|Acts 10:16⟧ σκεῦος refers to a sheet (as a container) which was let down from heaven in Peter’s vision.|In a number of languages there is no relatively high generic term which may be used to refer to any type of vessel or container, and therefore one must employ more specific terms depending upon the context, even as in the case of most English translations in ⟦Acts 10:11|Acts 10:11⟧, ⟦Revelation 2:27|Revelation 2:27⟧, and ⟦Luke 8:16|Luke 8:16⟧.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: objects which are possessed
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκεῦος<SDBG:σκεῦος:000000>}[a] ‘instrument, thing,’ {D:6.1}) a person in relation to a particular function or role

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Body
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκεῦος<SDBG:σκεῦος:000000>}[a] ‘object, thing, instrument,’ {D:6.1}, or of {L:σκεῦος<SDBG:σκεῦος:000001>}[b] ‘vessel,’ {D:6.118}) the human body
s.c: It is also possible to interpret σκεῦος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ as meaning ‘wife,’ and for a discussion of this meaning and some of the problems involved in translation, see LN 10.55. A further alternative meaning, and one closely related to the meaning of ‘body’ is ‘sexual life,’ so that this expression in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ might be rendered as ‘each of you must gain mastery over his sexual life’ or, in the form τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ, ‘your sexual life should be holy and honorable’ (see LN 23.63).

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκεῦος<SDBG:σκεῦος:000001>}[b] ‘vessel,’ {D:6.118}) a woman married to a man, with focus upon the sexual relation
s.c: The interpretation of σκεῦος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ has given rise to serious divisions of opinion as noted in LN 8.6, where σκεῦος is interpreted as designating a person’s own body. The interpretation of σκεῦος as ‘wife’ is based upon a number of considerations. In the first place, the verb κτᾶσθαι ‘to get, to acquire’ (LN 57.58) does not normally go with ‘body,’ while it fits well with the meaning of ‘wife.’ On the other hand, σκεῦος meaning ‘wife’ is nowhere else attested in Greek but is assumed in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ to refer to a wife primarily on the strength of the particular interpretation of the context, in which πορνεία ‘immorality’ (LN 88.271) in verse 3 and and ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας ‘with a lustful desire’ (LN 25.30) in verse 5 are assumed to point to the meaning of σκεῦος as ‘wife.’ In ancient Jewish literature a wife was euphemistically called a ‘vessel’ in contexts relating to sexual relations, and ‘vessel’ is a very common meaning of σκεῦος in Greek. If, therefore, one assumes a Semitic background for this Greek text, the statement in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ would refer to the need for sexual life to be both holy and honorable (see LN 23.63).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sexual Relations
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to possess a vessel) a euphemistic manner of referring to sexual relations
s.c: It is also possible to understand σκεῦος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ as one’s wife (see LN 10.55). σκεῦος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 4:4|1 Thessalonians 4:4⟧ may also be understood as one’s body, and therefore the phrase τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι may be rendered as ‘to control his own body’ (see LN 8.6).

s.d: a portable dwelling of cloth and/or skins, held up by poles and fastened by cords to stakes
s.c: In a number of languages ‘tent’ is simply ‘a house made of cloth.’ One should avoid terms which would imply a military tent or a temporary shelter used only on vacations or holidays. In OT times such tents were permanent dwellings of nomadic groups and were moved from place to place as livestock were transferred from one pasture area to another.

s.d: the relatively large tent used as a central place of worship by the Jews prior to the building of the Temple
s.c: In a number of languages σκηνή may be rendered as ‘the largest tent in which God lived’ or ‘the large tent for worshiping God’ or ‘the holy tent.’ In selecting a proper designation for σκηνή, it is important to indicate that the function of σκηνή was essentially the same as that of the Temple; it was only a different type of construction and not a difference of use or of religious relevance.|Since σκηνή refers to one unique object, it is essentially equivalent to a title.

s.d: a Jewish festival commemorating God’s provision during the wanderings in the wilderness
s.g: festival of the tabernacles; celebration of the tents
s.c: In some languages it may be useful to speak of the Festival of Tents as ‘the festival when people lived in tents.’

s.d: one who makes tents as an occupation

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Body
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of σκῆνος ‘tent,’ not occurring in the NT) temporary habitation in the human body
s.c: Only rarely can one preserve in translation the figurative meanings suggested by the terms σκῆνος and σκήνωμα. What is significant in such contexts is the temporary nature of the dwelling, and therefore the relatively brief time which the body is to serve the person who dwells in it. In some cases it may be relevant, therefore, to have a footnote to point out the temporal aspects of this figurative usage of σκῆνος and σκήνωμα .

s.d: to come to dwell in a place defined psychologically or spiritually (with the possible implication in some contexts of a temporary arrangement)
s.g: to take up residence; to come to reside; to come to dwell
s.c: In all of these contexts, σκηνόω and ἐπισκηνόω are essentially figurative in meaning, for they deal with spiritual existence and residence rather than human residence or dwelling. In translating one should, in so far as possible, try to preserve this important figurative relationship, since it expresses one of the most significant ways in which spiritual and human existence can be combined. In some languages, however, it may be necessary to employ an expression which means simply ‘to be in’ or ‘to continue with,’ since expressions for ‘living’ or ‘dwelling’ may be based upon terms which are too specific in meaning, for example, ‘to eat from the same pot’ or ‘to enter by the same door.’

s.d: a dwelling, with the implication of temporary duration
s.c: In ⟦Acts 7:46|Acts 7:46⟧ there is a complex textual problem in which the critical text has τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰακώβ ‘the house of Jacob’ (but in the figurative sense of ‘people’), but the Byzantine text reads τῷ θεῷ Ἰακώβ ‘the God of Jacob.’ It is only with this latter form of the text that σκήνωμα would mean an actual construction or dwelling. If one adopts the form of the critical text, then σκήνωμα would point to ‘a place to dwell,’ in other words, an area or region (see LN 85.77).

s.d: (derivative of {L:σκηνόω<SDBG:σκηνόω:000000>} ‘to take up residence,’ {D:85.75}) a place where one may dwell, with the possible implication in certain contexts of something which is of temporary duration
s.c: An alternative reading of the expression σκήνωμα τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰακώβ ‘dwelling place for the people of Jacob’ in ⟦Acts 7:46|Acts 7:46⟧ has θεῷ for οἴκῳ (see LN 7.8) and the consequent translation ‘a house for the God of Jacob.’|For another interpretation of σκήνωμα in ⟦2 Peter 1:14|2 Peter 1:14⟧, see LN 8.5.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Body
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκήνωμα<SDBG:σκήνωμα:000000>}[a] ‘temporary dwelling,’ {D:7.8}) temporary habitation in the human body
s.c: Only rarely can one preserve in translation the figurative meanings suggested by the terms σκῆνος and σκήνωμα. What is significant in such contexts is the temporary nature of the dwelling, and therefore the relatively brief time which the body is to serve the person who dwells in it. In some cases it may be relevant, therefore, to have a footnote to point out the temporal aspects of this figurative usage of σκῆνος and σκήνωμα .|It is also possible to interpret σκήνωμα in ⟦2 Peter 1:14|2 Peter 1:14⟧ as meaning a temporary habitation, though referring, of course, to the human body (see LN 85.77).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in a dwelling, see {D:7.8}) to be alive, with special emphasis upon physical existence on earth
s.c: Most languages have rather generic expressions for ‘life’ or ‘to live,’ but sometimes there are idiomatic expressions which may readily fit the types of contexts illustrated by ⟦2 Corinthians 5:6|2 Corinthians 5:6⟧ and ⟦2 Peter 1:13|2 Peter 1:13⟧, for example, ‘to have strength,’ ‘to have one’s eyes,’ and ‘to walk about on the earth.’

s.d: shade, as a shelter from light and the heat associated with light
s.c: A term for ‘shade’ as an area sheltered from the direct rays of the sun usually differs from a term for ‘shadow,’ which is cast by a particular object blocking rays of light (see LN 14.61).

s.d: the shape or shade cast by an object which blocks rays of light
s.c: In ⟦Luke 1:79|Luke 1:79⟧ (τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις ‘those living in the darkness and shadow of death’), σκιά may be interpreted as being used figuratively of a shadow cast by impending death, that is to say, death is personified in such a way as to suggest that it casts a shadow because of its nearness. One may, therefore, translate τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις as ‘those who live in the darkness of impending death,’ in which case σκιά becomes essentially equivalent to an expression of time.|In a number of languages a term for ‘shadow’ has a number of very important meanings. In some instances it is regarded as a part of personality which goes on to the next world, since a dead person no longer ‘casts a shadow.’ The shadow may also be regarded as a kind of counterpart of the personality, a type of alter ego. In cases of severe illness one may say ‘his shadow has walked away,’ and in many parts of the world the shadow of a person is an important element in the practice of black magic, for to damage a shadow may be regarded as a means of causing harm to a person.

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Archetype, Corresponding Type [Antitype]
s.d: a faint archetype which foreshadows a later reality
to leap or jump, as a possible expression of joy and happiness
s.g: to jump for joy; to leap for joy
s.c: For a difference of semantic focus see LN 25.134).|In ⟦Luke 1:41|Luke 1:41⟧ σκιρτάω may be regarded as an instance of figurative usage: ἐσκίρτησεν τὸ βρέφος ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτῆς ‘the baby leaped for joy in her womb.’|Though it may seem quite natural to speak of ‘leaping for joy,’ in some cultures this would not be a meaningful combination of words, for leaping might suggest anger, ritual exorcism (driving out demons), or preparation for war. It may, therefore, be necessary in some languages to translate ‘jump for joy’ merely as ‘be exceedingly glad.’ It may be particularly awkward to speak of a fetus jumping in the womb, for obviously it would simply be a rapid movement of the limbs and not actual change of location. Therefore, it may be better to translate in some instances ‘moved quickly to show joy’ or ‘… as a sign of happiness.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκιρτάω<SDBG:σκιρτάω:000000>}[a] ‘to jump for joy,’ {D:15.243}) to be extremely happy, possibly implying in some contexts actually leaping or dancing for joy
s.g: to be extremely joyful; to dance for joy
s.c: χάρητε ἐν ἐκείνω τῇ ἡμέρᾳ καὶ σκιρτήσατε ‘be glad when that happens and dance for joy’ ⟦Luke 6:23|Luke 6:23⟧, but see also LN 15.243 for a different semantic focus. The phrase ‘for joy’ clearly expresses ‘reason,’ and therefore it may be useful to translate ‘dance for joy’ as ‘dance because I am so joyful’ or ‘… so happy.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Stubbornness
s.d: pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate{N:001}
s.c: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

s.d: pertaining to being harsh and violent
s.c: For another interpretation of σκληρός in ⟦James 3:4|James 3:4⟧, see LN 76.15.

s.d: pertaining to being powerful or strong
s.c: For another interpretation of σκληρός in ⟦James 3:4|James 3:4⟧, see LN 20.3.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Act Harshly
s.d: pertaining to being harsh or possibly cruel in one’s behavior
s.c: In a number of languages σκληρός in ⟦Jude 1:15|Jude 1:15⟧ may be translated as ‘words that cause pain’ or idiomatically as ‘words that are like daggers.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Act Harshly
s.d: pertaining to being hard and demanding in one’s behavior

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Stubbornness
s.d: a stubborn attitude with regard to any change in behavior
s.c: In a number of languages stubbornness may be described as ‘refusing to change’ or ‘refusing to think differently.’ In some instances stubbornness may be expressed idiomatically as ‘one’s heart only sees one thing’ or ‘one’s heart is blind’ or ‘one who always says No.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Stubbornness
s.d: pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate{N:001}
s.c: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Stubbornness
s.d: to cause to be stubborn and obstinate, especially with regard to the truth
s.g: to make stubborn; to make obstinate
s.c: In the expression σκληρύνω τὰς καρδίας ‘to cause the hearts to be obstinate’ in ⟦Hebrews 3:8|Hebrews 3:8⟧, ⟦Hebrews 3:15|Hebrews 3:15⟧, ⟦Hebrews 4:7|Hebrews 4:7⟧, καρδία must be understood as ‘the inner self’ (see LN 26.3) and as such the addition of καρδία merely reinforces the meaning of the verb σκληρύνω.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Stubbornness
s.d: to be stubborn, in the sense of refusing to believe
s.g: to be stubborn; to be obstinate

s.d: pertaining to being crooked or winding

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Licentiousness, Perversion
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκολιός<SDBG:σκολιός:000000>}[a] ‘crooked,’ {D:79.90}) pertaining to being unscrupulous and dishonest
a sharp projection of a woody plant (though possibly a splinter of wood) with the implication of its causing injury and discomfort
s.c: In the NT σκόλοψ occurs only in the figurative expression σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί ‘thorn in the flesh,’ and this expression has been subject to a number of different interpretations (see LN 22.20).

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Experience Trouble, Hardship
s.d: (an idiom, literally: thorn in the flesh) something which causes serious trouble and difficulty
s.g: trouble; woe; suffering; serious inconvenience; thorn in the flesh
s.c: There are a number of different interpretations of σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:7|2 Corinthians 12:7⟧ (see discussion at LN 20.27).

s.d: to continue to regard closely
s.c: It is also possible to understand σκοπέω in ⟦Romans 16:17|Romans 16:17⟧ as being predominantly a mental process of paying close attention in order to be prepared to respond appropriately (see LN 27.58).

s.dp: Learn › Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκοπέω<SDBG:σκοπέω:000000>}[a] ‘to notice carefully,’ {D:24.32}) to be ready to learn about future dangers or needs, with the implication of preparedness to respond appropriately
s.g: to beware of; to watch out for; to pay attention to

s.d: to exert effort in continually acquiring information regarding some matter, with the implication of concern as to how to respond appropriately
s.g: to be aware of; to be concerned about; to consider

s.d: to keep on giving serious consideration to something
s.g: to ponder; to let one’s mind dwell on; to keep thinking about; to fix one’s attention on

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension To a Goal
s.d: that toward which movement or activity is directed
s.c: The context of σκοπός in ⟦Philippians 3:14|Philippians 3:14⟧ is highly figurative, and in some languages it may be better rendered as ‘what I seek to achieve’ or ‘what I wish to accomplish.’ For σκοπός in the idiom κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω, see LN 89.56.

s.d: to cause a group or a gathering to disperse or scatter
s.g: to scatter; to cause to disperse

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκορπίζω<SDBG:σκορπίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to scatter,’ {D:15.135}) to give or distribute generously or in abundance
s.g: to give generously; to distribute generously
s.c: In a number of languages ‘to give generously’ may simply be rendered as ‘to give much often,’ but one may sometimes employ such figurative expressions as ‘to give from a full heart’ or ‘to give without holding back anything.‘

s.d: terrestrial arachnid (eight-legged) with pincers and a poisonous sting at the end of its jointed tail, which it can hold curved over the back; grows to about 13 cm long; known for the pain and danger of its sting, and associated with harsh, inhospitable living conditions
s.c: In the two NT occurrences of σκορπίος (⟦Revelation 9:5|Revelation 9:5⟧), the emphasis is upon the stinging capacity of the scorpion, and if in a particular area of the world scorpions are not known, it is possible to use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a fierce, stinging, little creature.’

s.d: pertaining to being in a state of darkness
s.c: In some languages ‘dark’ may be most satisfactorily expressed as ‘without light.’

s.d: a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see {D:14.36})
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of ⟦Luke 23:44|Luke 23:44⟧ ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning {L:σκοτία<SDBG:σκοτία:000000>}[a] ‘darkness,’ {D:14.53}) the realm of sin and evil
s.g: evil world; realm of evil; darkness

s.dp: Know › Not Able To Be Known, Secret
s.d: pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
s.g: in secret; in private; secretly; privately

s.d: (derivative of {L:σκοτία<SDBG:σκοτία:000000>}[a] ‘darkness,’ {D:14.53}) to change from a condition of being light to one of being dark
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 9:2|Revelation 9:2⟧ it may not be difficult to speak of ‘the air becoming dark,’ since this would mean the space above the earth, but it may be difficult to speak of ‘the sun becoming dark.’ In the latter instance, for both ⟦Revelation 9:2|Revelation 9:2⟧ and ⟦Matthew 24:29|Matthew 24:29⟧, one may say ‘the sun will no longer shine’ or ‘the sun will not give its light.’|In place of ‘the air became dark,’ it is also possible to speak of ‘the sky will become dark.’

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκοτίζω<SDBG:σκοτίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to become dark,’ {D:14.55}) to become unable to perceive and thus unable to understand
s.g: to be incapable of perceiving; to not be able to understand
s.c: It is rare that one can combine the concept of ‘becoming dark’ with incapacity to understand or comprehend. Sometimes a parallel figure of speech may be employed by using an expression such as ‘to not be able to see.’ For example, in ⟦Romans 1:21|Romans 1:21⟧ it is sometimes possible to translate ‘their foolish minds became unable to see the truth,’ and in ⟦Ephesians 4:18|Ephesians 4:18⟧ it is sometimes possible to translate ‘they were not able to see with their minds.’

s.d: a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see {D:14.36})
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of ⟦Luke 23:44|Luke 23:44⟧ ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκότος<SDBG:σκότος:000000>}[a] ‘darkness,’ {D:14.53}) the realm of sin and evil
s.g: evil world; realm of evil; darkness
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦Colossians 1:13|Colossians 1:13⟧ σκότος is a figurative reference to the Devil or Satan, since ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους is in a parallel relationship with τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the gloom of darkness) the dark, gloomy nature of hell as a place of punishment

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the outer darkness) a place or region which is both dark and removed (presumably from the abode of the righteous) and serving as the abode of evil spirits and devils
s.c: In a number of languages this expression in ⟦Matthew 8:12|Matthew 8:12⟧ must be rendered as ‘they will be thrown outside where it is dark.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:σκότος<SDBG:σκότος:000000>}[a] ‘darkness,’ {D:14.53}) to change from a condition of being light to one of being dark
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 9:2|Revelation 9:2⟧ it may not be difficult to speak of ‘the air becoming dark,’ since this would mean the space above the earth, but it may be difficult to speak of ‘the sun becoming dark.’ In the latter instance, for both ⟦Revelation 9:2|Revelation 9:2⟧ and ⟦Matthew 24:29|Matthew 24:29⟧, one may say ‘the sun will no longer shine’ or ‘the sun will not give its light.’|In place of ‘the air became dark,’ it is also possible to speak of ‘the sky will become dark.’

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:σκοτόω<SDBG:σκοτόω:000000>}[a] ‘to become dark,’ {D:14.55}) to become unable to perceive and thus unable to understand
s.g: to be incapable of perceiving; to not be able to understand
s.c: It is rare that one can combine the concept of ‘becoming dark’ with incapacity to understand or comprehend. Sometimes a parallel figure of speech may be employed by using an expression such as ‘to not be able to see.’ For example, in ⟦Romans 1:21|Romans 1:21⟧ it is sometimes possible to translate ‘their foolish minds became unable to see the truth,’ and in ⟦Ephesians 4:18|Ephesians 4:18⟧ it is sometimes possible to translate ‘they were not able to see with their minds.’

s.d: worthless or unwanted material that is rejected and normally thrown out

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Σκυθία ‘Scythia,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Scythia, a region north of the Black Sea, and regarded by the GrecoRoman world as utterly pagan and uncivilized
pertaining to being sad and discouraged

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Cause Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to cause trouble or harassment
s.g: to trouble; to harass; to bother

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Experience Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to suffer trouble or harassment
s.g: to be troubled; to be harassed; to be bothered
s.c: In ⟦Luke 7:6|Luke 7:6⟧ σκύλλου can perhaps be best rendered in some languages by supplying a pronoun, for example, ‘do not bother yourself’ or ‘do not trouble yourself’ or even ‘do not cause yourself difficulty.’

s.d: that which is taken away by force, particularly in the case of war

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: pertaining to being eaten by worms (a reference to the occurrence of worms in ulcerous tissue)
s.c: In some languages it is important to make a clear distinction between intestinal parasites and the grubs of flies which feed on ulcerous tissue.

s.d: small, soft, legless, tube-shaped creatures that have no bones or shells. They typically feed on overripe fruit, rotting meat, and similar things; most are larvae that hatch from the eggs laid by flies or some beetles; symbols of uncleanness, decay, and death
s.c: In ⟦Mark 9:48|Mark 9:48⟧ the reference is clearly to the type of maggots which feed on refuse.|In a number of languages a very important distinction is made between three different types of worms: (1) maggots, (2) worms that live in the ground, so-called ‘earthworms,’ and (3) intestinal worms. It is essential that an appropriate term be employed in order to avoid meaninglessness or misunderstanding.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: (derivative of {L:σμάραγδος<SDBG:σμάραγδος:000000>} emerald, {D:2.33}) consisting of emerald, emerald-like, {S:06600400300034} (see {D:2.29})

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: emerald, green in color (see {D:2.29}).
the aromatic resin of certain bushes
s.c: Myrrh was used as one of the ingredients involved in the process of embalming a corpse. Most translators borrow a term for myrrh and then use some kind of marginal note to explain that myrrh was a valuable aromatic substance often used in preserving a corpse. See LN 6.204.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city on the west coast of Asia Minor
wine drugged with myrrh and used as a stupefying potion{N:001}
s.c: In general, ἐσμυρνισμένος οἶνος must be rendered by means of a phrase or a clause, for example, ‘wine which has been mixed with a drug called myrrh’ or ‘wine mixed with a drug to reduce pain.’ It is, of course, also possible to use an abbreviated phrase such as ‘myrrhed wine’ and then to place the explanation of its function in a marginal note.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city located near the Dead Sea and destroyed because of its evil; possible identification with Tel Hammam, northeast of the Dead Sea

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the son and successor of David
a stretcher or plank used for carrying a corpse to a place of burial
pertaining to a receptor

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a small piece of cloth used as a towel, napkin, or face cloth

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a follower of Jesus
the capacity to understand and, as a result, to act wisely
the content of what is known by those regarded as wise
knowledge which makes possible skillful activity or performance
s.c: It is also possible to interpret σοφία in ⟦1 Corinthians 1:17|1 Corinthians 1:17⟧ as wisdom which makes possible correct understanding (see LN 32.32).

s.d: a document or book containing wise sayings (as in the phrase ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the Wisdom of God,’ {S:04201104900010}, a possible reference to the OT or to apocryphal wisdom literature, possibly even a book which has been lost)
s.c: If one understands ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ as being a reference to a book, one could translate the statement in ⟦Luke 11:49|Luke 11:49⟧ as ‘for this reason, the book entitled The Wisdom of God has the words: …’ On the other hand, the phrase ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ in ⟦Luke 11:49|Luke 11:49⟧ may mean merely ‘God’s wisdom’ (LN 32.32), and therefore this expression in ⟦Luke 11:49|Luke 11:49⟧ could be rendered as ‘God in his wisdom said’ or ‘God, who is wise, said.’

s.d: to cause a person to have wisdom and understanding
s.g: to cause to understand; to cause to be wise; to make wise

s.d: (derivative of {L:σοφία<SDBG:σοφία:000002>}[c] ‘specialized knowledge, skill,’ {D:28.8}) to have specialized knowledge involving the capacity to produce what is cleverly or skillfully made
s.g: to know how to create skillfully; to know how to contrive cleverly

s.d: pertaining to specialized knowledge resulting in the skill for accomplishing some purpose
s.c: In some languages one may render the phrase ‘expert builder’ (⟦1 Corinthians 3:10|1 Corinthians 3:10⟧) as ‘one who knew just how to build best.’

s.d: pertaining to understanding resulting in wisdom
a person of professional or semi-professional status who is regarded as particularly capable in understanding the philosophical aspects of knowledge and experience
s.g: one who is wise; wise man

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a country at the western end of the Mediterranean Sea

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: to cause a person to shake violently in convulsions
s.g: to throw into convulsions; to throw into a fit

s.d: to wrap a child in swaddling clothes (long strips of cloth)
s.g: to clothe in strips of cloth; to wrap up in strips of cloth; to wrap in cloths

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Extravagant Living, Intemperate Living
s.d: to indulge oneself excessively in satisfying one’s own appetites and desires
to pull or drag, requiring force because of the inertia of the object being dragged
s.g: to pull; to drag; to draw

s.d: a Roman military unit of about six hundred soldiers, though only a part of such a cohort was often referred to as a cohort
a soldier who acts as a courier to carry confidential information
s.c: In ⟦Mark 6:27|Mark 6:27⟧ σπεκουλάτωρ may also have the meaning of ‘executioner’ (see LN 20.70).

s.d: one who carries out official executions on the basis of orders from military or government officials
s.c: It is also possible to interpret σπεκουλάτωρ (a borrowing from Latin) as meaning ‘courier,’ possibly a soldier who had special duties to carry messages of a confidential nature (see LN 33.196).

s.d: to pour out an offering as an act of worship or ritual observance
s.g: to pour a libation; to pour out an offering
s.c: In some languages it may be almost meaningless to speak of ‘a person being poured out,’ and therefore it may be more appropriate to translate this expression in ⟦Philippians 2:17|Philippians 2:17⟧ as ‘but if my blood is to be poured out upon the sacrifice.’ In ⟦Philippians 2:17|Philippians 2:17⟧ and in ⟦2 Timothy 4:6|2 Timothy 4:6⟧ (the other occurrence of σπένδω in the NT), the contexts are highly figurative.

s.d: the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
s.c: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, σπέρμα, σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:σπέρμα<SDBG:σπέρμα:000000>}[a] ‘seed,’ {D:3.35}) posterity, with emphasis upon the ancestors role in founding the lineage
s.c: See discussion at LN 10.28.

s.d: a derivative and imparted nature
s.g: nature; something of the nature of
s.c: If in some languages it is not possible to speak literally of ‘God’s nature,’ it may still be possible to render the second clause in ⟦1 John 3:9|1 John 3:9⟧ as ‘because something of what God is like is in him’ or ‘because he has in himself something of what God is like.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (idioms, literally: to raise up seed) the male role in begetting children
s.g: to beget; to procreate; to become the father of
s.c: In contexts such as ⟦Matthew 22:24|Matthew 22:24⟧, ⟦Mark 12:19|Mark 12:19⟧, and ⟦Luke 20:28|Luke 20:28⟧ it may be important to add a note concerning levirate responsibilities, that is to say, the requirement for a younger brother to beget children by a deceased older brother’s wife and the reckoning of such an offspring as being the descendant of the older deceased brother.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of a term based on the practice of birds in picking up seeds) one who acquires bits and pieces of relatively extraneous information and proceeds to pass them on with pretense and show
s.c: The term σπερμολόγος is semantically complex in that it combines two quite distinct phases of activity: (1) the acquiring of information and (2) the passing on of such information. Because of the complex semantic structure of σπερμολόγος, it may be best in some languages to render it as ‘one who learns lots of trivial things and wants to tell everyone about his knowledge,’ but in most languages there is a perfectly appropriate idiom for ‘a pseudo-intellectual who insists on spouting off.’ For a different focus on the meaning of σπερμολόγος in ⟦Acts 17:18|Acts 17:18⟧, see LN 33.381.

s.d: (a figurative expression, literally: one who picks up seed; originally a reference to birds picking up seed, but figuratively applied to a person who is an information scavenger) one who is not able to say anything worthwhile in view of his miscellaneous collection of tidbits of information
s.c: For another interpretation of σπερμολόγος in ⟦Acts 17:18|Acts 17:18⟧, see LN 27.19.

s.d: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy{N:001}
s.g: to hasten to; to hurry to; to do quickly
s.c: For another interpretation of σπεύδω in ⟦Acts 20:16|Acts 20:16⟧, see LN 25.74.

s.d: to cause something to happen soon
s.g: to cause to happen soon; to hurry up
s.c: It is also possible to render this meaning of σπεύδω in ⟦2 Peter 3:12|2 Peter 3:12⟧ as ‘doing your best to cause …’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort
s.c: For another interpretation of σπεύδω in ⟦Acts 20:16|Acts 20:16⟧, see LN 68.79.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes
s.d: a cave or den generally large enough for at least temporary occupation by persons (since such places were often used for habitation or refuge by those who were refugees or thieves, σπήλαιον has in certain contexts the connotation of a ‘hideout’)
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 6:15|Revelation 6:15⟧ the reference of σπήλαιον is literal, since people actually hid themselves in such caves. In ⟦Matthew 21:13|Matthew 21:13⟧, however, the reference is to the Temple, which has been made a kind of ‘cave’ or ‘den,’ and since the connotation of the term suggests a ‘hideout,’ this is obviously a reflection upon the activities and motivations of those who had commercialized the Temple in Jerusalem.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of σπιλάς ‘a rock or reef washed by the sea,’ not occurring in the NT) an unrecognized source of danger or peril
s.c: σπιλάς in ⟦Jude 1:12|Jude 1:12⟧ may also be understood as meaning ‘spot’ or ‘stain’ (see LN 79.57).

s.d: that which constitutes an unwanted spot or stain upon something
s.c: It is also possible that in ⟦Jude 1:12|Jude 1:12⟧ σπιλάς means an ‘unseen danger,’ in that it may refer to a rock which is mostly or completely covered by the sea (see LN 21.5).

s.d: that which constitutes an unwanted spot or stain upon something
to cause a spot or stain upon something

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: to experience great affection and compassion for someone
s.g: to feel compassion for; to have great affection for; love; compassion

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the inner parts of the body, especially the intestines
(figurative extension of meaning of {L:σπλάγχνον<SDBG:σπλάγχνον:000000>}[a] ‘intestines,’ {D:8.58}) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling{N:001}
s.c: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον, κοιλία, and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: experiencing great affection and compassion for someone
s.c: In ⟦Philippians 1:8|Philippians 1:8⟧ the phrase ἐν σπλάγχνοις Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ is ambiguous. It may mean ‘because of the compassion which Christ Jesus himself has for you’ or ‘… for me.’ On the other hand, it may also be interpreted as characterizing the kind of love which Paul has for the believers, for example, ‘how I long for all of you, even with the kind of love Christ Jesus himself has for you.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: one for whom there is deep affection or compassion

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be restricted in the bowels) to restrict one’s affection for someone
s.g: to not respond with affection to someone; to close one’s heart to
s.c: In ⟦2 Corinthians 6:12|2 Corinthians 6:12⟧ it is also possible to understand στενοχωρέομαι as meaning ‘to live with severe restrictions’ (see LN 37.18), and σπλάγχνα may be interpreted as a psychological faculty of intent and feeling (see LN 26.11).

s.d: a porous material used to absorb liquid
s.c: In the only type of NT context in which σπόγγος occurs (⟦Matthew 27:48|Matthew 27:48⟧; ⟦Mark 15:36|Mark 15:36⟧; ⟦John 19:29|John 19:29⟧), it serves as a container for cheap wine offered to Jesus on the cross.

s.d: a reference to a receptor of a message (with an added feature of emphasis in the form σύ)
a reference to the receptors of a message, whether oral or written (with an added feature of emphasis in the form ὑμεῖς)
